subject: Computer Networking
title: Net Neutrality Explained
description: A micro-lesson that makes Net Neutrality Explained usable.

hook.text: Should your ISP decide which websites load fast and which load slow? That's the net neutrality debate.

buildup.text: Net neutrality says all internet traffic should be treated equally. No fast lanes for those who pay more.

discovery.text: Without it, ISPs could slow down competitors or charge websites for priority access to customers.

twist.text: Some argue ISPs need flexibility to manage congestion. Others say that's a slippery slope to gatekeeping.

climax.text: Rules vary by country and change with each administration. The battle over net neutrality is far from settled.

punchline.text: Net neutrality asks: who controls the speed of the internet?

quiz.question: What does net neutrality require?
options: ISPs treat all internet traffic equally regardless of source
All websites must be free to access

details.summary: Net neutrality is the principle that ISPs should treat all internet traffic equally, without blocking, throttling, or charging more for specific content.
details.whyItMatters: Net neutrality determines whether the internet remains an open platform. Without it, ISPs control which content loads fast and which does not.
takeaways: Net neutrality requires ISPs to treat all traffic equally
Without it, ISPs could create paid fast lanes
The debate centers on innovation, competition, and free expression

faq.question: Why do ISPs oppose net neutrality?
faq.answer: ISPs want to charge content providers for priority delivery, creating new revenue streams. They argue that heavy users like Netflix should pay more since they consume most bandwidth. ISPs claim they need this revenue to fund network infrastructure investment.

faq.question: Has net neutrality been violated in practice?
faq.answer: Yes. ISPs have throttled Netflix and YouTube traffic. Comcast throttled BitTorrent. AT&T blocked FaceTime on cellular plans to push customers to more expensive plans. These incidents demonstrate why net neutrality rules exist and why enforcement matters.
